title: Birth in Palmer, Texas and learning piano from player-piano rolls
summary: Parker gives his birth details and says his farm parents were not musical. He taught himself at four by copying the notes of player-piano rolls and then phonograph records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: All right, ready to go. This is August 28th, 1963 in the Tulane Jazz Archive. Is that correct? Paul Crawford and Ed Kahn interviewing Naki Parker. Let's start at the beginning and get

where you were from, when you were born, and your real name. John Parker, 1918, August the 8th, Palmer, Texas. And were your parents musically inclined? No, we had a cotton farm out there and a player piano that I was interested in all my life and that's about how I got started.
You want to go into more detail on the early music?

We used to have itinerant musicians who'd come through there and from the beginning I'd learned how to play by copying the notes going down on the player piano. Put a roll in and see the notes going down and then make the same notes go down in the same combinations. Children have keenly, keen sensitivities and can watch things going on and can absorb more being children somehow than we as adults can. Innovations of immortality and all that. And as a child you can see keenly little patterns going down, patterns of notes and clusters and then make the same combinations. One, three, five is easy for a child to see uncluttered by our own activities and other fields and copy the same things and play just like the phonograph, just like the player piano roll did. From then we had an old sonora phonograph and I could get records for the phonograph and copy them much the same way by ear because I'd already had the authority of learning from the player piano rolls first. And that's how I started playing the piano, by copying the rolls and the records that I heard. And that's been, I guess, with me all my life. How old were you when you started copying the rolls? I was four. Mama was on the phone one time and she heard something, she heard something but she knew this wasn't exactly the roll because it wasn't quite as full as that but still sort of like that it came in and I was playing the piano, the same little piece that we had on the roll. What was the piece? I don't know. I think, I know one of these first things was Jesus lover of my soul and another thing was aggravating Papa. The old thing there I always liked Russell. Russell Robinson's playing in 1920, aggravating Papa came out and I remember that's one of the tunes
that I used to like mainly. What generally were the kind of roles that you had around the house?

Oh, we had old Hilo March and all those that were popular at the time. And, but I do remember that thing by Russell Robinson. And I was surprised to visit Trevor Titchener in St. Louis to see some, some beautiful Creole bells, a cakewalk. And that was one of the ones he put this on and I remembered that years ago this is an old tune that I had particularly liked and had played many, many times. We had old, all the old carry mills things and pieces like Snow Deer, Rufus on Parade, all the old cakewalks and early rags.
